vignette:
The Weight of Ink and Ash

Raymond is a 63-year-old Māori man who has spent the better part of four decades building a small but respected publishing house in Auckland. He is broad-shouldered and deliberate in his speech, the kind of man who chooses words carefully — professionally and personally. He has been married to his wife, Hinerangi, for thirty-one years. She is the one who finally persuaded him to seek help, after watching him become, as she put it, "a stranger who sleeps in our bed."

Three years ago, Raymond was attending an industry conference at a waterfront convention centre when a chemical storage facility two blocks away caught fire and triggered a series of explosions. The first blast shook the building without warning. Raymond was in a crowded breakout session when the ceiling partially collapsed and a fireball rolled across the sky outside the windows. In the chaos that followed — smoke filling corridors, people screaming, a colleague bleeding heavily from a head wound beside him — Raymond helped carry two people out before the structure became too unstable to re-enter. He stood on the street for nearly four hours watching the building burn, not knowing whether others were still inside. Seven people died that day. Raymond knew two of them.

In the weeks afterward, he told himself he was fine. He was a practical man. He went back to the office. He reviewed manuscripts. He took meetings. But the smell of anything burning — toast, a candle, a neighbour's backyard fire — would send him back to that street with a violence that frightened him. His heart would slam against his ribs, his hands would go cold, and for several minutes he would be entirely unreachable, standing in his own kitchen or car park, convinced on some cellular level that he was still there, that it wasn't over.

Sleep became a battlefield. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart racing, the details of the fire more vivid than his waking life. He has stopped sleeping in on weekends because the longer he stays in bed, the more likely the dreams are to return. He rises early and sits with the lights on, reading manuscripts he cannot concentrate on, waiting for morning to make the world feel solid again.

At work, Raymond's staff have noticed a change in him, though they don't name it. He is quicker to anger than he once was, particularly when deadlines are missed or when the office feels chaotic. He has cancelled three book launch events in the past eighteen months, citing scheduling conflicts that don't quite add up. The truth is that crowded, loud spaces — the kind that once energized him — now feel like threats. He scans exits. He sits with his back to walls. He leaves early.

He has quietly restructured much of his work to be done remotely, telling himself it is simply efficiency. He reviews submissions from home, conducts editorial calls by phone, and has delegated most in-person author meetings to his deputy. The publishing world he loved — the launches, the festivals, the ink-stained community of it — feels increasingly inaccessible to him, sealed off behind glass.

What troubles Raymond most, and what he speaks about with the most difficulty, is the guilt. He did not go back in after the second explosion. He has constructed and reconstructed that decision hundreds of times, and no version of it fully absolves him. He knows, intellectually, that going back in would likely have killed him. But intellect and the three o'clock dark are not on speaking terms.

Hinerangi tells him she misses his laugh. He tells her he is trying. Both of these things are true. He sits in the consulting room with his hands folded on his knees, a man who has spent his life giving other people's stories a spine and a cover, now uncertain how to hold the shape of his own.
